'''James Andrew Harris''' (March 26, 1932 – December 12, 2000) was an American [[Radiochemistry|radiochemist]] who was involved in the discovery of elements 104 and 105 ([[rutherfordium]] and [[dubnium]], respectively). Harris was the head of the Heavy Isotopes Production Group, part of the Nuclear Chemistry Division of the [[University of California, Berkeley]].  Harris is known for being the first [[African American]] to contribute to the discovery of new [[Chemical element|elements]].<ref name=":0">{{Cite web|url=http://www.cpnas.org/aahp/biographies/james-a-harris.html|title=James A. Harris|date=2002|website=www.cpnas.org|publisher=National Academy of Sciences|access-date=2016-04-04}}</ref>

==Personal life==
James A. Harris was born on March 26, 1932, in [[Waco, Texas|Waco]], Texas.<ref name=":1">{{Cite web|url=http://www.fofweb.com/History/HistRefMain.asp?iPin=AASM0073|title=James Andrew Harris: Nuclear Chemist|last=Brown|first=M.C.|website=www.fofweb.com|access-date=2016-04-04}}</ref> Harris' parents divorced when he was young, after which he moved to [[Oakland, California]] with his mother.<ref name=":0"/> Harris met his wife Helen at [[Huston–Tillotson University|Huston-Tillotson College]], where they were both completing their undergraduate studies; they were married in 1957 and had five children, Cedric, Keith, Hilda, Kimberly, and James II. Between the time of his graduation from college and his marriage, Harris was drafted and served in the [[United States Army|Army]] as a personnel supervisor specialist.<ref name=":2">{{Cite web|url=http://online.infobase.com/HRC/LearningCenter/Details/8?articleId=161567|title=Harris, James A.|last=|first=|date=2014|website=Online Infobase|publisher=Facts on File|access-date=}}</ref><ref name=":5">{{Cite journal|last=Frederick-Frost|first=Kristen|date=1 Mar 2021|title=The Life and Career of James Andrew Harris: Let's Ask More of History|url=https://pubs.acs.org/doi/10.1021/acs.jchemed.0c01054|journal=Journal of Chemical Education|volume=98|issue=4|pages=1242–1248|doi=10.1021/acs.jchemed.0c01054|bibcode=2021JChEd..98.1242F|s2cid=233776292|url-access=subscription}}</ref> His hobbies included [[golf]], traveling, and community activities.<ref name=":0" /> James A. Harris died of a sudden illness on December 12, 2000.<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://wacohistory.org/items/show/197 |title=James Andrew Harris |last=Burke |first=Anabel |website=Waco History |language=en |access-date=2019-05-02}}</ref>

== Education ==
James A. Harris graduated from [[McClymonds High School]] in [[Oakland, California]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://wacohistory.org/items/show/197|title = James Andrew Harris}}</ref>  After high school, Harris returned to [[Texas]] where he attended [[Huston-Tillotson College]] in [[Austin, Texas|Austin]].<ref name=":3">{{Cite web|url=https://webfiles.uci.edu/mcbrown/display/harris.html|title=James Andrew Harris: Nuclear Chemist|website=webfiles.uci.edu|access-date=2016-04-04|archive-date=2019-04-30|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190430234327/https://webfiles.uci.edu/mcbrown/display/harris.html|url-status=dead}}</ref> He initially entered college on a music scholarship, but switched to studying [[chemistry]] and received a bachelor of science degree in 1953.<ref name=":5" /><ref name=":2"/> In 1975, Harris received a master's degree in Public Administration at [[California State University]], Hayward. Harris was awarded an [[honorary doctorate]] from Huston-Tillotson College in 1973 for his co-discovery of [[rutherfordium]] and [[dubnium]].<ref name=":3"/> Harris was also a brother of the African-American [[Alpha Phi Alpha]] fraternity.<ref name=":3"/>

== Career ==
Harris' first job in chemical research was as a [[Radiochemistry|radiochemist]] at [[Tracerlab Inc.]], a commercial research lab in [[Richmond, California]]; he worked there for five years.<ref name=":6">{{Cite journal|date=26 Mar 2018|title=James A. Harris|url=https://physicstoday.scitation.org/do/10.1063/pt.6.6.20180326a/full/|access-date=24 Feb 2022|journal=Physics Today|doi=10.1063/pt.6.6.20180326a|url-access=subscription}}</ref> Harris left Tracerlab Inc. to work on isotope division in the nuclear chemistry department of the [[Lawrence Radiation Laboratory]] at [[University of California, Berkeley|University of California-Berkeley]].<ref name=":1" /> His early work at the lab involved studying [[beta decay]] in the Beta Spectroscopy Group. He also worked on a project to improve [[neutron activation analysis]] with [[germanium]] [[Semiconductor|semiconducting]] detectors.<ref name=":5" /> Harris then joined the Heavy Isotopes Production Group on the team tasked with producing new heavy elements via atom bombardment. Harris' job was to design and purify targets that would be used in Berkeley's Heavy Ion [[Linear particle accelerator|Linear Accelerator]] to discover elements 104 and 105. These targets needed minimal impurities of elements such as [[lead]] to work.<ref name=":4">{{Cite web|url=https://www2.lbl.gov/Publications/Currents/Archive/Jan-26-2001.html|title=Jim Harris left his mark on science and community|last=Gonzales|first=Lisa|date=2000|website=Berkeley Lab Currents|publisher=Berkeley Lab|access-date=}}</ref> Harris' colleagues praised his work, saying that it was high quality and very good for [[heavy element]] research.<ref name=":4" /> He and his colleagues also conducted what they called the “first aqueous chemistry of element 104”, to determine how the new element behaved and thus where it should be placed on the periodic table.<ref name=":5" />

Two research teams were simultaneously working to discover elements 104 and 105. One was Harris's team at the University of California-Berkeley and the other was a team of Russian scientists. Both teams successfully isolated the two elements around the same time in 1969 and 1970, so there is dispute over which team was actually the first to isolate the elements. In 1997 the [[International Union of Pure and Applied Chemistry]] settled the dispute: element 104 was given the name suggested by the American research team, rutherfordium, after the [[Ernest Rutherford|influential British physicist]]. Element 105 was subsequently given the name dubnium, representing the city, [[Dubna]], where the Russian team worked.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://classroom.synonym.com/african-american-nuclear-scientist-discovered-elements-rutherfordium-hahnium-11265.html|title=Who was the African American Nuclear Scientist who discovered the Elements Rutherfordium & Hahnium?|last=Green|first=John|publisher=|access-date=April 4, 2016}}</ref>

As head of the Heavy Isotopes Production Group, Harris and his team continued the search for other heavy elements which might be more stable and therefore useful for medicine, energy, or other purposes.<ref name=":7">{{Cite web|last=Johnson|first=Bethany|date=28 Oct 2020|title=James Andrew Harris (1932-2000)|url=https://www.blackpast.org/african-american-history/james-andrew-harris-1932-2000/|access-date=24 Feb 2022|website=Black Past}}</ref> Six years after discovering elements 104 and 105, Harris took a position with the Berkeley Lab Office of Equal Opportunity. There he worked with Benjamin Pope to recruit more women and minorities to work at the lab, focusing on outreach at [[Historically black colleges and universities|Historically Black Colleges and Universities]] (HBCUs) and forming partnerships with engineering colleges.<ref name=":5" /> In 1977, Harris was promoted to Head of Engineering and Technical Services Division.<ref name=":3" /> He retired in 1988.

During his career and after retirement, Harris worked with students in grade school and at the university level to encourage African Americans students into the sciences. This work earned him numerous awards from organizations including the National Organization for Equal Opportunity in Education, the [[Urban League]] and the [[National Organization for the Professional Advancement of Black Chemists and Chemical Engineers]].<ref name=":6" /><ref name=":7" />

== Awards ==
* Honorary PhD from [[Huston-Tillotson College]] (1973)
* Scientific Merit Award from the Mayor of [[Richmond, California|Richmond, CA]]
* Certificate of Merit from the Black Dignity Science Association

== Organizations==
Harris was a part of the following organizations:<ref name=":1"/>

* [[National Organization for the Professional Advancement of Black Chemists and Chemical Engineers|National Society of Black Chemists and Chemical Engineers]]
* Nuclear Target Society
* [[American Chemical Society]]
* AEC Transplutonium Program
* [[Alpha Phi Alpha]] fraternity
